title: Insert Interval
description: Brute force to optimized: appending and re-sorting/re-merging versus a single pass through three zones exploiting the already-sorted input.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time, and a new interval newInterval, insert newInterval into the array, merging any overlaps, so that intervals remain sorted by start time with no overlaps. Return the resulting array.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Since the existing intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, inserting a new interval only requires finding where it fits: intervals entirely before it stay as they are, intervals overlapping it get merged into one combined interval, and intervals entirely after it stay as they are, all identifiable in a single pass without re-sorting.

blocks.title: Analogy: Inserting a New Reservation into an Already-Organized Schedule
blocks.text: Picture an already neatly organized, non-overlapping reservation schedule, and needing to insert one new reservation that might overlap a few existing ones. Rather than rebuilding the entire schedule from scratch, you can walk through it once: keep everything before the new reservation as is, merge everything it overlaps into one combined block, then keep everything after as is.

blocks.caption: Three zones in a single pass: intervals before, intervals overlapping (merged), intervals after

blocks.text: Result: [[1,5],[6,9]]. [1,3] overlaps [2,5], merging into [1,5]; [6,9] does not overlap and stays separate.

Before treating this as a general "add one interval, then re-merge everything," notice that the existing intervals are ALREADY sorted and merged, so a single pass can directly identify the three zones (before, overlapping, after) without needing to re-sort anything.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since intervals are already sorted by start time, all intervals ending strictly BEFORE newInterval starts can simply be copied to the result as is (zone 1).

Observation 2: Any interval whose start is at or before newInterval's (possibly already-extended) end OVERLAPS it and should be merged in, expanding newInterval's bounds to cover it (zone 2).

Observation 3: Once no more intervals overlap the (possibly expanded) newInterval, that merged interval is added to the result, and every remaining interval is copied as is (zone 3), since they all start after it ends.

Observation 4: This entire process is a single linear pass through intervals, since each interval is examined and classified into exactly one zone exactly once.

This leads to a single pass: copy intervals ending before newInterval starts; merge all intervals overlapping newInterval, expanding its bounds; append the merged interval; then copy the remaining intervals.
Append newInterval to the existing list, then re-run a full Merge Intervals (sort plus single-pass merge) on the combined list from scratch.

items: Append newInterval to the end of the existing intervals list.
Sort the entire combined list by start time.
Run the standard single-pass merge over this newly sorted list.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Re-sorting and re-merging the whole list directly reuses the Merge Intervals solution, correct but wasteful.
This costs O(n log n) due to the full re-sort, ignoring that the original list was already sorted before adding just one new interval.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the unnecessary re-sort.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: since the original intervals were already sorted, a single O(n) pass (without any sorting) can directly insert and merge the new interval, avoiding the O(n log n) re-sort entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-sorting is unnecessary: the existing intervals are already in sorted, merged form; only ONE new interval is being added, so its correct position and overlaps can be found directly in a single linear scan.

The three-zone single pass: copy every interval ending strictly before newInterval starts (zone 1, unaffected); then, while the current interval's start is at or before newInterval's (possibly expanding) end, merge it in by expanding newInterval's bounds (zone 2); once this stops, append the merged newInterval, then copy every remaining interval (zone 3, unaffected).

Why this correctly reproduces the merged result: each interval is examined exactly once, and its correct treatment (copy or merge) is fully determined by its relationship to the single newInterval, without needing global re-sorting.

The core idea: exploit the already-sorted structure with a targeted single pass, avoiding the unnecessary O(n log n) sort.
In a single pass: copy intervals ending before newInterval's start; merge all intervals overlapping newInterval (expanding its bounds); append the merged interval; copy the remaining intervals.

blocks.caption: A single pass through the three zones correctly inserts and merges the new interval

codes.python:
def insert_interval(intervals, new_interval):
    result = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new_interval[0]:      # zone 1: entirely before
        result.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    start, end = new_interval
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= end:                    # zone 2: overlapping, merge
        start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
        end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append([start, end])
    while i < n:                                                 # zone 3: entirely after
        result.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    return result

blocks.text: Since the input is already sorted and non-overlapping, every interval falls cleanly into exactly one of three zones relative to newInterval: entirely before it (copied unchanged), overlapping it (merged into its expanding bounds), or entirely after it (copied unchanged). Because the intervals are processed strictly in order, this classification never needs to be revisited, so a single linear pass correctly produces the final sorted, merged result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with no sorting needed.
Space: O(n) for the result.

blocks.text: Insert Interval demonstrates that exploiting an ALREADY sorted input can turn an O(n log n) re-sort-and-merge into a direct O(n) single pass, by explicitly reasoning about the three zones relative to the newly inserted element.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "insert one new item into an already-sorted, already-merged structure", think: a single targeted pass exploiting the existing order, avoiding any unnecessary re-sort.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The append-and-re-sort approach costs O(n log n) time; the single-pass three-zone approach costs O(n) time, both using O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a single targeted pass through three zones (before, overlapping, after), exploiting an already-sorted input.
Core Idea: copy intervals before newInterval unchanged; merge all overlapping intervals into its expanding bounds; copy intervals after unchanged.
Time: O(n log n) for append-and-re-sort, O(n) for the optimized single pass.
Most Important Observation: exploiting that the input is already sorted avoids the need for any re-sort when inserting just one new interval.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known interval problem testing whether "already sorted" is recognized and exploited.
One line memory trick: copy before, merge overlapping, copy after, in one pass.
